posts.title: What we look at on a 45-minute roof visit
posts.excerpt: A roof visit takes about 45 minutes and most of it is looking up.
posts.content:
A roof visit takes about 45 minutes and most of it is looking up. We check the condition of the tiles or shingles, the pitch and orientation of each slope, and what shades it between nine and three.

Indoors we look at the meter and the fuse board, because they decide how a system can be connected. A week later you get it all in writing, including the assumptions behind every estimate.

posts.title: Does a battery pay for itself? Our honest maths
posts.content:
A 13.5 kWh battery from $10,900 stores midday surplus for the evening. Whether it pays for itself depends on your tariff, how much you use after six and what your export rate is.

For many households it does not pay back quickly, and we say so. It makes sense when evening use is high, when you want backup for a few essential circuits, or when export rates are poor.

posts.title: Cleaning panels: when to bother, and when not to
posts.excerpt: Rain does most of the cleaning for you.
posts.content:
Rain does most of the cleaning for you. If the panels are tilted at 15 degrees or more and there is regular rain, leave them alone.

Clean them if birds, pollen or a nearby building site leave a film, and do it from the ground with water and a soft brush. Never go onto the roof for it; our $190 annual visit covers it safely.

posts.title: How long from yes to switch-on?
posts.excerpt: Most homes are switched on four to eight weeks after a signed proposal.
posts.content:
Most homes are switched on four to eight weeks after a signed proposal. The roof work is the short part, usually one to three days.

The rest is waiting: the permit, the parts, and the network operator’s inspection. We tell you which step we are on and what we are waiting for.

posts.title: Flat roof or pitched: what changes for a business
posts.excerpt: On a flat roof we prefer ballasted frames that need no holes in the membrane.
posts.content:
On a flat roof we prefer ballasted frames that need no holes in the membrane. On a pitched roof we fix to the structure and seal every penetration.

Both start with a structural check, and both are priced per watt. A flat roof often costs a little less to fit but needs more panels for the same output at a low tilt.

posts.title: Five numbers worth checking in your proposal
posts.excerpt: Look for the system size in kW, the estimated yearly output in kWh, the rate used to turn it into a saving, the installed price and the warranty terms.
posts.content:
Look for the system size in kW, the estimated yearly output in kWh, the rate used to turn it into a saving, the installed price and the warranty terms.

If any of the five is missing, ask. A good proposal shows its assumptions, and ours say plainly that savings are estimates, not guarantees.
